findings.paper_title: Council Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Underspend driven partly by one-off parking charge increase and temporary corporate items (£4m balance sheet clearing)
findings.detail: The Place directorate underspend of £5.1m was 'primarily driven by increased income within Parking' due to 'a Londonwide decision to increase PCN charges' implemented after budget setting. Corporate savings of £23.7m included one-off items: £1m contingency release and £4m from 'review of the balance sheet clearing historic suspense items'. These do not recur, so the underlying position is less favourable than reported outturn.
findings.matters: A lender reviewing this result needs to understand which savings are sustainable; reliance on PCN charge increases (external decision) and one-off balance sheet items suggests the sustainable deficit is larger
findings.figures: £5.1m underspend in Place; £4m one-off balance sheet clearing; PCN income from London-wide charge decision
findings.quote: The Place Pillar underspend was primarily driven by increased income within Parking in the Environment Pillar primarily due to a Londonwide decision to increase PCN charges. The cross London Fee increases in penalty charges commenced in April 2025, post budget setting, generating additional income.

findings.paper_title: Council Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Planned revenue savings of £1.2m not achieved and £2.0m delayed into 2026/27, to be written out of future budgets
findings.detail: Of £10.2m planned savings for 2025/26, the council delivered £7.0m but failed to achieve £1.2m and delayed £2.0m. The report states these will be 'written out of the 2026/27 budget with departments asked to contain spend in a sustainable fashion within their assigned budgets in order to achieve this.' This signals difficulty executing savings plans and adds to 2026/27 pressure.
findings.matters: Failed or delayed savings indicate departments cannot deliver planned efficiencies, forcing either deeper cuts elsewhere or higher borrowing/support requirements
findings.figures: £1.2m savings not achieved; £2.0m delayed from £10.2m target
findings.quote: A number of savings however were not achieved and the resultant overspend is included within the revenue outturn position reported in this report. Some of these savings proposals are simply delayed and will be achieved in 2026/27 whilst others will not be delivered.

findings.paper_title: Council Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Schools shifted from £1.86m surplus to £0.72m deficit with 15 schools now in deficit totalling £6.3m
findings.detail: Havering's 38 maintained primary and 1 maintained special school shifted dramatically: overall position moved from £1.86m surplus to £0.72m deficit (a £2.58m swing). Within this, 15 schools are in deficit with a combined deficit of £6.3m. The council attributes this to funding not keeping pace with pay and cost rises, plus high special educational needs costs. Schools have been required to produce recovery plans but no timeline for return to balance is stated.
findings.matters: Schools in persistent deficit signal underlying service demand exceeding available funding; this typically requires council bailouts from general fund or indicates inability to fund statutory services adequately
findings.figures: 15 schools in deficit with total of £6.3m; overall shift of £2.58m from £1.86m surplus to £0.72m deficit
findings.quote: the level of balances held by schools at the end of the financial year decreased from a total of £1.86m surplus to an overall deficit of £0.72m – a fall of £2.58m. Within this overall total there were 15 schools in deficit with a total of £6.3m

findings.paper_title: Council Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: £240m of internal borrowing outstanding with external borrowing expected to be needed in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council states that 'general fund capital internal borrowing still stands at over £240m at year end' and notes 'It is highly likely therefore that further new external borrowing will be needed in 2026/27 both to finance that years capital programme but also to reduce the level of internal borrowing as those funds are needed for other purposes.' This represents a substantial debt accumulation.
findings.matters: A lender tracks total debt exposure and the capacity to service it; £240m internal borrowing being converted to external borrowing will materially increase annual debt service costs over 20 years
findings.figures: £240m internal borrowing; further external borrowing needed 2026/27
findings.quote: general fund capital internal borrowing still stands at over £240m at year end. It is highly likely therefore that further new external borrowing will be needed in 2026/27 both to finance that years capital programme but also to reduce the level of internal borrowing as those funds are needed for other purposes.

findings.paper_title: Council Revenue and Capital Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Underlying structural deficit requiring £37.7m exceptional financial support in 2025/26 and £77m budgeted for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's revenue outturn shows a £37.7m overspend against original budget without exceptional financial support. This is not a one-off variance but an underlying structural gap: the council explicitly states it 'has no alternative but to set budgets using exceptional financial support as a balancing item'. For 2026/27, the budget is already underpinned by a £77m capitalisation directive request.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a deficit is temporary or structural; this is clearly structural and will persist, requiring repeated government bailouts
findings.figures: £37.7m deficit 2025/26; £77m capitalisation directive budgeted 2026/27
findings.quote: The overspend however is an underlying budget gap and so therefore forms part of the 2026/27 requirement for further exceptional financial support.

findings.headline: Council used internal borrowing to delay external borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The council reduced the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) budget by £1.1m due to capital slippage, but more significantly used internal borrowing to defer external borrowing for both Exceptional Financial Support and general Capital spend. The savings from reduced borrowing costs (£6.1m) were achieved through this internal borrowing approach, which delays but does not eliminate the future external borrowing requirement.
findings.matters: A lender would see this as drawing down reserves to avoid external borrowing now, with the consequence that borrowing need will be larger or more urgent in future years. This is a timing risk management decision with future consequences.
findings.figures: £6.1m saving from reduced external borrowing costs through internal borrowing
findings.quote: The Council has used internal borrowing to delay the need for external borrowing for both EFS and general Capital spend resulting in a GF underspend.

findings.headline: Council wrote back £3.5m of unmatched historic receipts and £0.5m of suspense items from balance sheet review
findings.detail: As part of the outturn process, the council undertook a balance sheet review and identified historic accounting items: £0.5m of suspense items and £3.5m of unmatched receipted items. These were written back to revenue to support the outturn position, suggesting historical record-keeping or control gaps.
findings.matters: A lender would view this as a potential control weakness and flag that the council's records are not clean. Using balance sheet write-backs to improve revenue position also raises questions about the reliability of the overall position.
findings.figures: £0.5m suspense items; £3.5m unmatched receipts; £4.0m total write-back
findings.quote: As part of the outturn process the Council undertook a balance sheet review and identified £0.5m of historic suspense items and £3.5m of unmatched historic unmatched receipted items. These items have been written back to revenue to support the Council's outturn position

findings.headline: Multiple savings programmes delayed or requiring formal policy changes
findings.detail: Savings delivery is patchy across People and Place pillars. In People: delayed savings on Foster Carer Recruitment, Supported Living, Temporary Accommodation, and the Family Welcome Centre; some activity (Reablement) contributing to cost avoidance rather than cashable savings. In Place: the Voluntary Sector rental contribution saving is unachieved and requires formal policy change to deliver. In Corporate: the Business Rate Pool generated £0.8m against a forecast of £1.2m (£0.4m shortfall).
findings.matters: A lender would see savings plans failing to land or requiring external policy change (especially Place), reducing trust in the council's forecasting and indicating deeper structural issues.
findings.figures: Corporate savings shortfall £0.5m; Business Rate Pool benefit £0.8m vs forecast £1.2m
findings.quote: There are delayed People savings relating to Foster Carer Recruitment, new Supported Living and Temporary Accommodation including the Family Welcome Centre and some further potential savings in Adult Social Care from targeted reviews and transition planning. The unachieved saving in Place relates to the Voluntary Sector rental contribution and will require a formal policy change.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation underspend is one-off and the area remains flagged as a risk
findings.detail: Temporary Accommodation shows an underspend, but this is driven entirely by one-off backdated Housing Benefit income from 2024/25 and one-off grants. The report explicitly states the service remains a risk area despite the underspend, implying underlying cost pressures will resurface once the one-offs end.
findings.matters: A lender would recognise this underspend as temporary cover masking a demand pressure that will return. The next year should see costs rise back to budgeted levels or higher.
findings.figures: Underspend driven by backdated HB income and one-off grants
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation also remains a risk area despite the underspend due to the underspends being one offs from backdated Housing Benefit income due from 2024/25 realised in year and one-off grants.

findings.headline: Learning Disabilities service overspent by £1.95m despite receiving £4.9m growth allocation
findings.detail: Within Living Well, Learning Disabilities overspent by £1.95m in a year when the service received £4.9m of additional growth funding. The overspend reflects high-cost transition cases and increasing levels of client complexity. The report notes that complexity pressures continue to be an area of concern.
findings.matters: A lender would see a service that cannot be controlled despite receiving new money, with worsening demand/complexity. This suggests future growth will not fix the underlying problem.
findings.figures: £1.95m overspend against £4.9m growth
findings.quote: Within Living Well Learning Disabilities has overspent by £1.95m, reflecting the impact of high‑cost transition cases and increasing levels of client complexity, despite adding in £4.9m of growth. Complexity pressures continue to be an area of concern.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant has accumulated £69m deficit; council faces unspecified future £6.9m local contribution
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £32.235m this year (16.4% of budget), driven by High Needs Block costs (£34.837m overspend despite Havering being least-funded council in London). The accumulated deficit now stands at £69m. DfE announced a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of this, but approval depends on the council's SEND Reform Plan being approved by DfE, and the remaining 10% (forecast £6.9m) must be funded locally at an unspecified time.
findings.matters: A lender would see a £69m ringfenced deficit as destroying reserves and creating contingent future liability. Funding the 10% shortfall is uncertain and could arrive at any point. The council's DSG crisis is acute and worsening.
findings.figures: £69m total DSG deficit; £32.235m current year overspend; £34.837m High Needs Block overspend; £6.9m forecast local contribution required
findings.quote: The DSG is a ringfenced line within the Council's reserve which now stands at £69m total deficit (including this year's overspend.) However, the remaining 10% will require a local contribution to be made at an unspecified time. This is forecast to be £6.9m should the plan be approved by the DfE.

findings.headline: Council required £37.7m of exceptional financial support despite services underspending budget
findings.detail: The final outturn was £242.11m total net expenditure, which was £37.7m above available funding even though services collectively came in under budget. Services and corporate budgets delivered underspends, but the council still relies on exceptional financial support to balance. This reveals a structural gap between the council's spending envelope and its funding.
findings.matters: A lender would see this as demonstrating the council's budget cannot be balanced without government bailout, despite management action. This is not a one-year issue but reflects fundamental funding pressure.
findings.figures: £242.11m outturn vs £204.39m available funding before exceptional support; £37.7m gap
findings.quote: The final outturn position for the Council was total net expenditure of £242.11m which is £37.7m over the available funding necessitating the use Exceptional Financial Support.

findings.headline: HRA staff capitalisation policy decision: £1.2m of professional support costs deemed non-capitalisable
findings.detail: Within HRA Stock, £1.2m of "professional support services where numerous members of staff originally forecast to be capitalised were deemed to not meet the capitalisation criteria." Expected capital treatment did not materialise; costs now treat as revenue instead, shifting budget pressure.
findings.matters: Staff costs that cannot be capitalised reduce capital benefit and increase revenue pressure; indicates either forecast accuracy issues or that capitalisation policies are tighter than council expected
findings.figures: £1.2m professional support services reclassified from capital to revenue
findings.quote: Key Slippages are as a result of professional support services (£1.2m) where numerous members of staff originally forecast to be capitalised were deemed to not meet the capitalisation criteria

findings.headline: Resourcing constraints prevented Transport for London schemes delivery, resulting in unrecovered grant funding
findings.detail: On TfL-funded schemes (part of £1.376m TfL slippage), council explicitly states: "Resourcing constraints, meaning some planned schemes were not delivered and funding was not claimed." This is not timing slippage but lost grant funding due to inability to staff project delivery.
findings.matters: Resource constraints preventing scheme delivery indicate staffing/expertise gaps; lost grant funding because council cannot deliver is a revenue loss affecting future budgets and questions delivery capacity
findings.figures: Part of £1.376m TfL slippage
findings.quote: Resourcing constraints, meaning some planned schemes were not delivered and funding was not claimed.

findings.headline: Farnham & Hildene commercial acquisition project stalled pending GLA funding confirmation
findings.detail: Phase 1 of Farnham & Hildene commercial acquisitions suffered £5m slippage because project "did not commence due to delay in confirmation of the GLA funding pushing back the project by several months." Project is entirely dependent on partner funding confirmation to proceed.
findings.matters: Project stalled waiting for external partner funding confirmation indicates funding uncertainty or discussion delays; dependency on GLA funding creates risk if conditions or priorities change
findings.figures: £5m slippage, several months delay
findings.quote: Slippage of £5m on Phase 1 Farnham & Hi ldene commercial acquisitions which did not commence due to delay in confirmation of the GLA funding  pushing back the project by several months.

findings.headline: Emmanuel Community Free School funding held up due to third-party contractor non-performance
findings.detail: £600k of council funding to Emmanuel Community Free School on Beam Park development has not been paid over because "works to build the nursery and SEND unit have not yet been started by the 3rd party." Council has paid its capital contribution but third-party contractor has not commenced works, withholding funds.
findings.matters: Council funding held pending third-party performance creates cash flow and delivery risk; indicates weak control over development partners; third-party delays can cascade into future year pressures
findings.figures: £600k funding withheld, not yet claimed
findings.quote: There has also been delays in the Emmanuel Community Free school on the Beam Park housing development where £600k of funding has yet to be paid over to the school as the works to build the nursery and SEND unit have not yet been started by the 3rd party.

findings.headline: SEND school expansion projects delayed due to procurement and contractor appointment issues
findings.detail: Multiple statutory SEND (Special Educational Needs & Disabilities) school projects suffered £2.862m slippage, attributed to "delays in the procurement process and appointment of contractors." Affected schemes: SEND units at Brittons Academy, Lime Academy expansion, Harrow Lodge Primary, and Gidea Park. Spend now deferred to 2026-27.
findings.matters: SEND provision is a statutory duty; procurement delays in this protected area increase legal/reputational risk; suggests procurement capacity constraints affecting multiple schemes simultaneously
findings.figures: £2.862m slippage across four SEND school projects
findings.quote: The school's slippage has predominantly been caused by delays in the procurement process and appointment of contractors for the SEND unit at Brittons Academy, Lime Academy expansion, the Harrow Lodge Primary Send unit and the expansion of Gidea Park.

findings.headline: 12 Estates regeneration project (3,500-home target) behind schedule with approval process bottleneck identified
findings.detail: This major housing regeneration joint venture suffered £3.091m slippage despite £24m spend in 2025-26 alone. Council reports project is "behind schedule" with explicit bottleneck: "The process of approving the valuation is likely to continue until the end of July and then the project will be back up to speed." This suggests governance/approval delays blocking progress on a major initiative.
findings.matters: Approval delays on a major housing regeneration project targeting 3,500 new homes indicate governance constraints; delays compound costs and defer revenue; the specific July deadline suggests ongoing constraint
findings.figures: £3.091m slippage, £24m spent in 2025-26 on 3,500-home programme
findings.quote: The project is behind schedule but is still progressing on site with spend now anticipated in 2026/27 . The process of approving the valuation is likely to continue until the end of July and then the project will be back up to speed.

findings.headline: Mercury Land Holdings (council development company) delayed start on four housing schemes due to approval and funding release delays
findings.detail: The council's wholly-owned development company planned to start four schemes in 2025-26 (Peel Way, Albert Road, Dorrington Gardens, Keswick Avenue) but suffered £5.112m slippage. Council explicitly states: "business case approval and funding release took longer than the profile assumed." Two other schemes (Priory Road, Quarles) also underperformed.
findings.matters: Internal approval delays on the council's revenue-generating development company indicate governance bottlenecks; the company is central to housing supply and revenue strategy, so delays affect financial sustainability
findings.figures: £5.112m slippage, four schemes delayed, smaller underspends on two others
findings.quote: The slippage reflects a delayed start on site at four schemes approved to start in 2025/26 (Peel Way, Albert Road , Dorrington Gardens and Keswick Avenue), plus slower than  profiled progress at Priory Road and Quarles, which are under construction. The starts have run behind the P9 profile because business case approval and funding release took longer than the profile assumed.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £28.4m less than forecast, driven by project delivery delays and approval bottlenecks
findings.detail: Total 2025-26 capital expenditure was £135.353m against forecast of £163.721m. The council is requesting carry forward of £125m to 2026-27. Slippages affected schools SEND expansions, housing regeneration schemes, and transport projects across multiple directorates, with specific reasons including procurement delays, internal approval bottlenecks, and third-party dependency.
findings.matters: A 17% underspend against a quarterly forecast indicates systematic project delivery challenges; large carry-forwards create recurring budget pressure and question the reliability of future year forecasts
findings.figures: £28.368m variance, outturn £135.353m vs forecast £163.721m, carry forward £125m
findings.quote: In 2025/26 there is a variance of £28.368 m (as set out in table 3.1) between the period 9 forecast reported and the final outturn of £135.353m.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84718/Treasury Management Annual Review report 2025-26 AC meeting 30 June 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Net debt increased by £85m in the year as the council both increased borrowing and depleted investment reserves
findings.detail: The council's net debt (gross borrowing minus investments) rose from £490.6m to £576m, driven by £23m of new debt and £62m reduction in investments. This dual movement reflects both capital programme funding pressures and the strategy of using internal resources to defer long-term borrowing.
findings.matters: Rising net debt combined with depleting liquid reserves is a key indicator of increasing financial leverage; lenders use this pattern to assess deterioration in financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Net debt increased £85.4m; composition: £23.4m new borrowing, £62m reduction in investments
findings.quote: The Net Debt position (gross borrowings less investments) has increased in year by £85m. £23m of this relates to an increase in actual debt taken out in year and £62m from a reduction in investments resulting in higher levels of internal borrowing.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84718/Treasury Management Annual Review report 2025-26 AC meeting 30 June 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Investment portfolio has halved to £55m and liquidity buffer reduced to £40m minimum as reserves are drawn to fund operations
findings.detail: Cash investments declined by £62m during the year (from £117m to £55m), deployed to fund capital expenditure and capital programme slippage relief. The council now maintains a minimum £40m liquidity buffer for contingencies, indicating tighter financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Shrinking liquid reserves and a tightened contingency buffer reduce the council's ability to absorb cash flow shocks or market disruptions; this is a leading indicator of financial stress.
findings.figures: Investments fell from £117m to £55m (£62m reduction); minimum liquidity buffer £40m
findings.quote: Officers kept treasury investments in short-term instruments in 2025/26 less than 1 year so they could be used to fund the capital programme whilst maintaining a liquidity buffer of £40m as a contingency against any future credit crisis.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84718/Treasury Management Annual Review report 2025-26 AC meeting 30 June 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Management explicitly states the current borrowing strategy requires reassessment in 2026/27 due to increasing interest rate volatility
findings.detail: The council has deferred long-term fixed-rate borrowing in favour of internal cash reserves, saving £3.6m in capital finance costs in 2025/26. However, the report states this strategy 'increases interest rate volatility and will require reassessment during 2026/27', signalling that the approach is acknowledged as unsustainable if conditions do not improve.
findings.matters: A fundamental strategy reassessment on the horizon indicates the current financing model has limits; this directly impacts medium-term borrowing costs and affordability.
findings.figures: Net interest underspend £3.6m in 2025/26; internal borrowing of £179m against CFR of £810m
findings.quote: The current approach of deferring long-term borrowing increases interest rate volatility and will require reassessment during 2026/27.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84718/Treasury Management Annual Review report 2025-26 AC meeting 30 June 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Over half the council's debt matures within two years, creating significant refinancing exposure as interest rates have risen
findings.detail: The council's debt maturity profile shows 26.41% due within 12 months and 29.72% between 12-24 months, totalling 56% of the £631m portfolio. In February-March 2026, the council borrowed £320m in 1-2 year loans at 4.07% to refinance £297m of maturing debt during a period when gilt yields spiked following Middle East tensions.
findings.matters: Refinancing half the debt portfolio in 24 months exposes the council to materially higher borrowing costs if rates remain elevated; this directly affects affordability and the sustainability of the capital programme.
findings.figures: £631m total debt; 56% matures within 24 months (£166.6m under 12 months, £187.5m 12-24 months); £320m new PWLB borrowing Feb-March 2026 at 4.07%
findings.quote: During the period February 2026 through to March 2026 new 1-2 year PWLB loans were taken totalling £320m at an average rate of 4.07%.

findings.headline: Head of Assurance opinion improved from Limited to Reasonable Assurance year-on-year
findings.detail: 2024/25 opinion was Limited Assurance due to significant issues including suspected fraud and control failures. 2025/26 opinion has improved to Reasonable Assurance, with remaining issues isolated to specific service areas and no systemic control weaknesses identified.
findings.matters: Improvement in assurance opinion suggests governance remediation is working, though the baseline (Limited Assurance) was weak; context matters — prior year had suspected fraud.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Head of Audit Opinion for 2024/25 concluded that... only Limited Assurance could be provided... In contrast, based on audit work undertaken during 2025/26, the Head of Assurance is able to provide Reasonable Assurance that the Council maintains a generally sound system of internal control.

findings.headline: Procurement governance arrangements flagged as weak and at risk of being compounded by resource shortages
findings.detail: The AGS identifies procurement governance as a significant issue with identified weaknesses. The statement notes that ongoing strengthening of arrangements may be compounded by resourcing issues, poor link to commissioning, and changes to delegation scheme and regulations during 2024.
findings.matters: Weak procurement governance increases the risk of contract overspend, poor value, and challenge to spending decisions; compounding factors (staffing shortages, regulatory change) suggest the weakness is worsening not improving.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Procurement: Continuing to strengthen the governance arrangements for procuring goods and services may be compounded by resourcing issues, effective link in with commissioning, and changes to the scheme of delegation and new regulations during 2024.

findings.headline: Starting Well children's services received an Inadequate Ofsted rating in December 2023
findings.detail: The AGS flags an Inadequate judgement outcome from Ofsted's inspection of Havering's local authority children's services in December 2023. This is listed as a significant governance issue requiring monitoring.
findings.matters: An Inadequate Ofsted rating in children's services triggers intervention, reputational damage, and often requires emergency funding for improvement; this signals governance and management risk that could prompt intervention by the Department for Education.
findings.figures: Inspection date: December 2023
findings.quote: Inadequate judgement outcome of Starting Well's Social Care Department following Ofsted's Inspection of Local Authority Children's Services (ILACS) in December 2023.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation Service had significant control failure with budget management weaknesses
findings.detail: The Head of Assurance opinion specifically names the Temporary Accommodation Service as having had a significant control failure, with evidence of weaknesses in budget management, inconsistent application of financial controls, and insufficient management oversight.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a rising cost pressure across English councils; control failures here signal both budget exposure and weak oversight in a volatile spend area.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: significant control failure within the Temporary Accommodation Service, highlighting weaknesses in budget management, inconsistent application of financial controls, and insufficient management oversight

findings.headline: Control failures across three service areas in 2024/25 resulted in financial loss to the Council
findings.detail: The AGS identifies multiple control failures towards the end of 2024/25 involving inconsistent application of financial controls and poor management oversight. These failures led to financial inefficiencies and misallocation of resources, with actual financial loss incurred. Both first and second lines of defence failed.
findings.matters: Demonstrable control failures and financial losses signal weak financial governance and risk management; repeated control breakdowns across multiple areas suggests systemic weakness rather than isolated incident.
findings.figures: No quantified loss disclosed
findings.quote: A number of control failures were identified towards the end of 2024/25 across three service areas... ultimately resulting in financial loss to the Council.

findings.headline: Council unable to demonstrate a balanced budget solution for 2026/27
findings.detail: Identified as a significant governance issue in the 2025/26 AGS. The document does not provide detail on the scale or solution, only that this is a flagged concern requiring monitoring.
findings.matters: Budget delivery risk directly impacts a council's creditworthiness and ability to service debt; unresolved budget gaps suggest either spending cuts or reserve drawdown ahead.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Delivery of a balanced budget 2026/27

findings.paper_title: App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026 , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84726/App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026.pdf
findings.headline: IT systems migration in November 2025 caused access delays for council officers to their own systems and audit portal
findings.detail: The council migrated away from OneSource systems in November 2025. This resulted in access issues for council officers to the council's own systems, supporting documentation and evidence, and to EY's client portal, delaying responses to audit queries.
findings.matters: This is both a symptom and cause of weak financial reporting infrastructure. It shows the council's systems are fragile enough that migration causes significant operational disruption mid-audit cycle.
findings.figures: Migration occurred November 2025
findings.quote: the Council in November was impacted by changes in IT systems due the Council migrating away from OneSource systems. This resulted in access issues for Council officers, to the Council's own systems and supporting documentation/evidence and access to EY's client portal, delaying responses to audit queries during this period

findings.paper_title: App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026 , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84726/App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Council's rebuilding timeline has fallen behind NAO expectations; unqualified opinion unlikely before 2027/28 at earliest
findings.detail: The audit plan compares the council's progress to the NAO's Local Audit Reset and Recovery Implementation Guidance (LARRIG). The council is behind expected recovery timescales. The auditors assess it is unlikely audit assurances can be rebuilt to enable an unqualified opinion in 2026/27.
findings.matters: The path out of financial audit risk is now 4+ years away (2028 at earliest). This signals deep, systemic issues in financial reporting capability that cannot be remedied quickly.
findings.figures: Disclaimed 2024/25, likely disclaimed 2025/26, qualified opinion unlikely until 2026/27 at earliest
findings.quote: In our view, the Council's progress falls behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01. As set out in our 2024/25 Audit Results Report this means it is unlikely that audit assurances can be rebuilt to enable an unqualified opinion in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026 , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84726/App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026.pdf
findings.headline: £66.2 million bad debt provision remains unaudited due to complexity and historic data access
findings.detail: The council's bad debt provision for 2024/25 was £66.2 million across multiple categories (council tax, NNDR, housing, benefit, parking, sundry). Auditors could not complete planned procedures in 2024/25 due to complexity of the provision and inability to access the historic data from 2017/18 that underpins it. This remains a heightened misstatement risk.
findings.matters: £66.2 million is material to the financial statements. If unaudited and unsupported, it represents a direct misstatement risk to the balance sheet. The inability to access underlying data suggests systems or record-keeping issues.
findings.figures: £66.2 million total bad debt provision (2024/25)
findings.quote: The Council's Bad Debt provision (impairment) for 2024/25 was £66.2 million, comprising of several individual elements each requiring Management to make a number of accounting judgements as to the recoverability of debt. In 2024/25, we were unable to complete our planned procedures over the Bad Debt Provision due to the complexity of the provision and access to the historic data upon which the provision is calculated.

findings.paper_title: App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026 , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84726/App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026.pdf
findings.headline: 20% of audit working papers missed agreed deadline in 2024/25, creating audit execution risk
findings.detail: Approximately 20% of working papers were not provided to the agreed timetable, particularly those for debtors and creditors. The auditors also note delays in provision of supporting evidence and quality issues requiring significant requests for clarification.
findings.matters: Failure to meet audit deadlines and provide quality working papers delays completion of the audit and increases risk of incomplete audit opinion. This is a structural issue, not one-time.
findings.figures: 20% of working papers late; IT system migration in November impacted further responses
findings.quote: Approximately 20% of working papers in 2024/25 were not provided to the agreed timetable

findings.paper_title: App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026 , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84726/App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Internal audit opinion of limited assurance with suspected frauds and control weaknesses not yet remedied
findings.detail: The 2024/25 Head of Internal Audit opinion was limited assurance due to control weaknesses linked to suspected frauds. This was reported as a significant weakness in governance arrangements. The audit plan notes a continuing risk that the council has not made adequate progress in addressing these weaknesses.
findings.matters: Suspected fraud combined with limited assurance on internal controls indicates material risk of financial loss or misstatement. Lenders require evidence of strong governance; this suggests it is absent.
findings.figures: 2024/25 Head of Internal Audit opinion: limited assurance
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Head of Internal Audit's audit opinion was one of limited assurance, highlighting weaknesses in the Councils internal control linked to a number of suspected frauds. Following our VFM work in 2024/25 we determined that a significant weakness existed in the Councils governance arrangements.

findings.paper_title: App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026 , item 5.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84726/App A London Borough of Havering - Provisional Audit Plan - 30 April 2026.pdf
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion likely to persist into 2025/26 due to unresolved prior-year gaps
findings.detail: The auditors state it is unlikely they will move away from a disclaimed audit opinion for 2025/26. The council has received disclaimed opinions in both 2023/24 and 2024/25 due to inability to obtain assurance over opening balances and key transactions. Planned audit procedures remain incomplete for debtors, creditors, other expenditure and reserves.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the auditor cannot form any opinion on the financial statements at all. This signals fundamental issues with the council's financial reporting systems or records that persist despite two years of audit effort.
findings.figures: 2023/24 and 2024/25 disclaimed; 2025/26 likely also disclaimed
findings.quote: it is likely that we would not be able to gain sufficient audit assurance to move away from a disclaimed audit opinion outcome, though will keep this under review during our audit

findings.paper_title: HEAD OF ASSURANCE ANNUAL OPINION 2025-26 & INTERNAL AUDIT PLAN OUTTURN
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s84721/Head of Assurance Annual Opinion 2025 26 incorporating Internal Audit Plan Outturn Cover Report.pdf
findings.headline: Council had financial control and oversight weaknesses in 2024/25 that required management action
findings.detail: The report notes an improved position from 2024/25 following action on financial control and oversight weaknesses. The current Head of Assurance opinion is 'reasonable assurance', confirming a generally sound control environment, but the explicit reference to prior year weaknesses indicates the council had identifiable gaps in its financial systems.
findings.matters: Lenders assess councils' financial management capability through the strength of their internal controls. Prior weaknesses in financial control indicate areas where financial reporting or budget management could have been compromised; understanding what those weaknesses were and whether they are fully resolved is material to credit assessment.
findings.figures: None provided in this summary document
findings.quote: Improved position from 2024/25, following action on financial control and oversight weaknesses

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s83254/14.0 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report - P10.pdf
findings.headline: General reserves forecast £20.2m against adequacy target of £27m; reserves declining over medium term
findings.detail: The council targets 10% of net spend (£27m) as general reserves for adequacy. It currently holds £15.2m budgeted to increase to £20.2m by end of 2025/26. This falls £6.8m short of target. Additionally, total earmarked reserves are declining: opening at £40.0m for 2025/26, forecast to £31.1m by year-end, £29.4m by 26/27, and £27.3m by 27/28. This drawdown pattern indicates reserves are being consumed faster than regenerated.
findings.matters: Reserves below adequacy target and declining over time indicate the council is drawing down buffers to manage structural deficits. This reduces financial resilience to unexpected shocks and limits ability to invest in change.
findings.figures: Current £15.2m, budgeted £20.2m general reserves vs £27m target (10% of £275m spend); earmarked reserves declining from £40.0m (opening) to £27.3m by 27/28
findings.quote: The Council currently has £15.2m of General Balances and has budgeted to increase this value to £20.2m in 2025/26. The current net spend is £275m and therefore approximately 10% would require a General Balance of £27m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s83254/14.0 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report - P10.pdf
findings.headline: Adult social care overspend driven by rising number and complexity of new clients; savings initiatives underperforming
findings.detail: Living Well services forecasting £2.3m overspend (£2.6m Adult Social Care, £1.1m Housing Demand). The paper states 'the Social Care pressures mostly arise from the number of new clients and the complexity of their needs which has resulted in an overspend forecast.' Critically, 'the savings achieved from initiatives such as Better Living and targeted reviews have not been in line with targets.' The underlying demand pressure is structural and the council's mitigation strategies are failing.
findings.matters: Social care is typically a council's largest controllable spend. Uncontrolled demand growth and ineffective savings initiatives signal that the demographic and complexity drivers are outpacing management action. This is a leading indicator for future budget pressure.
findings.figures: £2.3m Living Well overspend; £2.6m Adult Social Care element; demographic-driven, not temporary
findings.quote: the Social Care pressures mostly arise from the number of new clients and the complexity of their needs which has resulted in an overspend forecast. In addition, the savings achieved from initiatives such as Better Living and targeted reviews have not been in line with targets.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s83254/14.0 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report - P10.pdf
findings.headline: Ten maintained schools in severe financial difficulty with £8.25m deficit; six more schools newly unable to balance budgets
findings.detail: Of 38 maintained and voluntary aided schools, 10 are in 'severe financial difficulty' with £8.25m cumulative deficit and 'severe and enduring pressures that we have not yet been able to resolve.' Additionally, 6 schools newly unable to balance budgets in 2025/26 beyond the 15 schools already in deficit at end of 2024/25 (£6.48m deficit). The average maintained primary school budget is £3.3m, meaning the system deficit represents 2.5+ schools' worth of spending.
findings.matters: School deficits represent a governance and service delivery risk. The paper shows the problem is worsening (6 new deficit schools added), and the council's recovery plans are not resolving the 'severe and enduring' pressures. This signals either funding inadequacy or management issues that extend beyond the council's control.
findings.figures: 10 schools in severe difficulty (£8.25m); 15 schools in deficit at end 24/25 (£6.48m); 6 newly unable to balance; average school budget £3.3m
findings.quote: Schools in severe financial difficulty 10 (£8.25m) these schools have severe and enduring pressures that we have not yet been able to resolve.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s83254/14.0 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report - P10.pdf
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reaches £67.7m with demand outstripping grant funding growth
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is forecasting a £31.5m in-year overspend, bringing cumulative deficit to £67.7m. The paper states 'The pressure on this budget is driven entirely by demand for additional support which has been increasing very sharply over recent years and is outstripping the increase in grant funding.' The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of accumulated deficits, but Havering's 10% local contribution is around £6.7m.
findings.matters: This structural, demand-driven deficit shows no sign of stabilising. Even with government grant support, the council must fund a £6.7m local contribution. This is a long-standing overspend pattern, not temporary, and reflects demographic/policy pressures the council cannot control.
findings.figures: £31.5m forecast in-year overspend; £67.7m cumulative deficit; £6.7m local contribution required
findings.quote: There is a forecast overspend of £31.5m on the High Needs Block which is available to fund the costs of support for pupils with Special Educational Needs. This block has been overspending for a number of years now and by the end of the year the cumulative deficit is expected to be £67.7m

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s83254/14.0 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report - P10.pdf
findings.headline: Three-quarters of required savings delivered; remainder uncertain and expected to miss target
findings.detail: Of £10.2m MTFS savings required in 2025/26, only £7.47m has been 'entirely delivered' by end of January. The remaining £2.78m are 'highly uncertain and not expected to be delivered in year.' This includes £0.5m shortfall on corporate savings (£0.2m agency levy, £0.3m Business Rate Pool) and delays in People services savings including Family Welcome Centre, supported living units, and new family support delivery models.
findings.matters: Savings underperformance indicates that the council's strategy to close its structural deficit is not working as planned. If savings continue to miss targets, the EFS requirement will grow.
findings.figures: £10.2m required; £7.47m delivered; £2.78m uncertain; £0.5m corporate shortfall
findings.quote: The remaining £2.78m of savings are highly uncertain and are not expected to be delivered in year. These include two Corporate savings (the agency levy saving (£0.2m) and the Business Rate Pool £0.3m) which are likely to underachieve creating a £0.5m shortfall.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report 2025/26.
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s83254/14.0 Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring Report - P10.pdf
findings.headline: Council cannot set a balanced budget without government support despite end-of-year forecast underspend
findings.detail: Although forecasting a £17.4m underspend at P10, this masks a structural deficit: the council still requires £53m of Exceptional Financial Support for 2025/26. This pattern has persisted for multiple years. The budget was set requiring 'at least £70.2m of Exceptional Financial Support... with the worst-case potential of £88.0m.' This is not a temporary issue but reflects chronic underfunding relative to demand.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can operate sustainably. Reliance on exceptional government support signals underlying structural deficit that could affect creditworthiness if support is withdrawn.
findings.figures: £53m EFS required; £70.2m minimum EFS needed; £88.0m worst-case EFS
findings.quote: This will require use of £53m of Exceptional Financial Support. The DSG is forecasting an in year overspend that will bring the total deficit to £67.7m.

findings.headline: The council is raising council tax by the maximum permitted amount (4.99%) in each year of the medium-term plan, indicating financial constraint rather than choice
findings.detail: The council is implementing the maximum council tax increase allowed by law: 2.99% general increase plus 2% Adult Social Care precept. This is not a discretionary policy choice but a necessary step to balance the budget. The council cannot increase council tax further without a referendum. This signals severe financial pressure and leaves no room for Council Tax policy flexibility in future years if the structural deficit persists.
findings.matters: A council already raising council tax at the maximum legal rate has exhausted this revenue source. If the council's deficit widens further, it will have no flexibility to raise additional income from council tax without breaching referendum requirements. This removes a key tool for addressing future deficits.
findings.figures: 4.99% council tax increase (2.99% + 2% ASC precept) at legal maximum; Council Tax requirement £174.421m
findings.quote: Given the financial situation set out in this report the Council has little alternative but to recommend the maximum 4.99% increase in Council Tax

findings.headline: The council has explicitly stated that 'the scope to identify significant new savings is extremely limited' and its unit costs are already low compared to neighbouring authorities
findings.detail: In discussing its £10m savings proposals for 2026/27, the council notes: 'The Council has relatively low unit costs compared to its neighbours and further cuts would directly impact on service delivery.' This indicates the council has already cut to the bone and has little remaining flexibility to find new savings without materially reducing services. This constrains the council's ability to solve its structural deficit without external support or fundamental service redesign.
findings.matters: A council that cannot identify additional savings is one that cannot address its structural deficit through efficiency alone. Any lender must assume that future gaps will require either: (a) continued emergency government funding, (b) further service cuts impacting service quality, or (c) further council tax increases beyond the legal maximum (which cannot happen). This points to an unsustainable long-term position.
findings.figures: £10m savings identified for 2026/27, but council acknowledges severely limited scope for further savings
findings.quote: It should be noted that the scope to identify significant new savings is extremely limited. The Council has relatively low unit costs compared to its neighbours and further cuts would directly impact on service delivery

findings.headline: The council estimates it will need £25m of budget by 2028/29 simply to service the debt and financing costs of Exceptional Financial Support, representing 30% of the projected gap
findings.detail: The council is borrowing heavily through Exceptional Financial Support to balance its budget. By 2028/29, the financing costs of this EFS borrowing alone are estimated at £25m — that is, 30% of the total budget gap will be consumed simply paying interest and principal on emergency borrowing rather than funding services. This creates a vicious cycle: the larger the EFS, the larger the financing costs, the larger the future gap.
findings.matters: This reveals a deeply unsustainable financial trajectory. The council is not addressing the underlying deficit through service redesign or demand management; instead, it is borrowing to cover the gap, which increases future deficits. Within three years, a quarter of the gap will be pure financing costs, leaving less room to actually solve the underlying problem.
findings.figures: £25m financing costs by 2028/29 = 30% of total gap; total gap before EFS 2028/29 £82.3m
findings.quote: By 2028/29 it is estimated that the Council will need to include £25m of budget simply to finance the borrowing and repayment costs of EFS. This is around 30% of the total gap for that year

findings.headline: The council's general balances are amongst the lowest in London and the risk mitigation reserves are projected to decline to £7.8m by March 2028
findings.detail: Havering's general balances have been depleted in recent years through pressures on services and are amongst the lowest in London. The council is attempting to rebuild general balances to a target of £25m, currently at £20.2m (end 2025/26). However, risk mitigation reserves (held for unforeseen pressures) are projected to decline from £16.8m (opening 2025/26) to £11.3m by end March 2026, £10.0m by end March 2027, and £7.8m by end March 2028, indicating shrinking financial resilience.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion signals a council consuming its financial buffers to meet current operational costs. By 2028, the council will have very limited capacity to absorb any unexpected financial shocks — redundancy liabilities, one-off costs, service pressures — and may be forced to further cut services or draw down balances further.
findings.figures: General balances £20.2m (forecast end 2025/26) target £25m; Risk mitigation reserves declining from £16.8m to £7.8m by March 2028
findings.quote: Havering recognises the need to have adequate reserves and balances and maintains a £1m corporate contingency for unforeseen in year pressures. Havering's general balances and earmarked reserves have been depleted in recent years through the pressures on services and are amongst the lowest in London

findings.headline: Children's services staffing costs have jumped £5.5m in two years following Ofsted requirements, and the borough is experiencing the highest population growth of young people in the country
findings.detail: Havering has experienced 6% population growth in children since 2020 (double the next-largest increase among Outer London boroughs) and the 4th highest growth in young people in the country. The council is receiving a net inflow of children from neighbouring boroughs. Following an Ofsted report, the council restructured and reduced social worker caseloads, but overall staffing costs in children's social care rose from £22.5m in 2023/24 to £28m budgeted for 2025/26. Additionally, EHCPs have risen 12% per year for the last 3 years, driving home-to-school transport costs.
findings.matters: This is a fundamental demographic problem for the council: children are arriving in the borough faster than average, requiring more services, and Ofsted has mandated staffing increases to meet safeguarding standards. These are non-discretionary costs that will persist for years as cohorts age through services.
findings.figures: Children's social care staffing: £22.5m (2023/24) to £28m (2025/26); EHCP growth 12% per year for 3 years; 6% child population growth since 2020
findings.quote: Havering has had 10.4% population growth from 2011 to 2021 which has outpaced the London average of 7.7% However Havering's 6% rise in children since 2020 is double the next largest increase among Outer London boroughs. Havering has the 4 th highest growth in young people in the Country. The number of EHCP's has risen by an average of 12% per year for the last 3 years. The Council's recent OFSTED report identified the need for the Council to reduce its caseload per social worker and invest in a number of key posts. The overall staffing cost of children's social care has risen from £22.5m in 2023/24 to a budget of £28m in 2025/26

findings.headline: Adult social care costs are escalating sharply: one-to-one support placements have quadrupled in cost and residential care weekly rates are up 67% in four years
findings.detail: The number of adult social care users requiring 1-to-1 support increased from 80 people costing £2.5m in 2020/21 to 236 people costing £9.6m in 2024/25. The average weekly cost of a residential placement rose from £630 in 2021 to £1,050 in 2025. The council's provider contracts total over £110m, meaning a 1% price increase equals £1m in additional cost. The council attributes this to National Living Wage increases (35% over 5 years), increased complexity of need, and a shortage of bed spaces driving up market prices across North-East London.
findings.matters: Adult social care represents one of the fastest-growing cost drivers in the council's budget. With an aging population and provider shortages, these costs are largely outside the council's control and will continue to rise. The £110m provider contracts create exposure to inflationary pressures.
findings.figures: 1-to-1 support: 80 people (£2.5m) in 2020/21 to 236 people (£9.6m) in 2024/25; residential care: £630/week (2021) to £1,050/week (2025); provider contracts £110m+
findings.quote: The Councils provider contracts now total over £110m which means even a 1% increase in prices results in over £1m additional costs. 35% increase in the National Living Wage over the last 5 years. Significantly increased complexity of care – The number of users requiring 1-2-1 support has increased from 80 in 2020/21 (cost £2.5m) to 236 in 2024/25 (cost £9.6m). The average weekly cost of a residential placement has risen from £630 in 2021 to £1050 in 2025

findings.headline: Temporary housing placements have tripled from 3 to over 300 people, creating an additional ongoing cost of over £8m annually
findings.detail: Housing demand has surged from 200 monthly approaches in 2021 to 300 monthly approaches now. As a result, the number of people in nightly lets and hotels rose from just 3 in 2020 to over 300 now, representing an additional net spend of over £8m. Meanwhile, the number of private sector leasing properties available to the council fell from 750 in 2021 to 400 now due to government rent caps, reducing housing options.
findings.matters: This is a structural demand-driven cost, not a temporary spike. The shrinking PSL market and inability to reduce placements suggests the council faces long-term housing costs that will only grow. This is a core driver of the structural deficit and cannot be easily managed down.
findings.figures: 300+ people in temporary accommodation vs 3 in 2020; £8m+ additional net spend; PSL properties 400 now vs 750 in 2021
findings.quote: The number of approaches has increased from 200 per month in 2021 to 300 now. As a result, the numbers in nightly lets and hotels has risen from just 3 in 2020 to over 300 now (additional net spend over £8m)

findings.headline: The council faces budget deficits totalling £82.3m by 2028/29 even after receiving £39m in new grant and raising council tax by 4.99% each year
findings.detail: Despite the Fair Funding Review increasing grant by approximately £39m over three years and the council maximising council tax increases at 4.99%, the Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows a structural deficit that grows: £65.9m (2026/27), £81.6m (2027/28), £82.3m (2028/29). The council's demand-led pressures exceed what government has provided in additional funding.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit despite maximising available revenue sources indicates the council's cost base is unsustainable. The gap cannot be closed through further council tax rises (already at legal maximum) or savings alone, creating permanent reliance on government emergency support.
findings.figures: £65.9m gap 2026/27, £81.6m gap 2027/28, £82.3m gap 2028/29; demand pressures £19.0m in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: Note that the medium term financial strategy presented in this report still leaves a financial gap of £82.3m in 2028/29 even after the full impact of the fair funding review grant increases and a 4.99% Council tax increase for the next three years have been applied

findings.headline: Without Exceptional Financial Support and Capitalisation Direction, the council will be required to issue a Section 114 report declaring it cannot set a balanced budget
findings.detail: The council cannot balance its 2026/27 budget without obtaining a Capitalisation Direction from government (allowing revenue expenditure to be charged to capital). If the Direction is not awarded before 4 March, the S151 Officer must issue a Section 114 report. The council is explicitly dependent on government emergency funding to function.
findings.matters: A Section 114 report is a formal declaration that a council cannot set a balanced budget — the most severe financial warning a local authority can issue. For any lender, this signals extreme distress and inability to meet obligations.
findings.figures: £65.9m mid-case budget gap for 2026/27 requiring EFS; £77.0m worst-case gap
findings.quote: in the event the Capitalisation Direction is not awarded to the value requested before the Full Council meeting on the 4th March, the Strategic Director of Resources (S151 Officer) will be required to issue a S114 report

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: Regeneration borrowing is growing but remains the only source of offsetting revenue income
findings.detail: Regeneration borrowing is rising steeply (£90.6m to £245.8m over 4 years) but is presented as sustainable because the projects generate rental and other income to offset costs. This income stream is critical to the overall affordability case.
findings.matters: If regeneration projects underperform or face delivery delays, the income assumptions will collapse and the affordability model fails. Asset value and market risk are embedded in the projections.
findings.figures: Regeneration CFR 2024/25: £90.6m; 2028/29: £245.8m; financing cost ratio under 5% of Council Tax yield (2028/29: 8.0%)
findings.quote: Regeneration borrowing climbs higher rising from £90m to £246m over the same time period however this supports a large programme of regeneration which, whilst not being the primary objective, generates significant revenue income to offset the financing costs

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: Council plans to refinance short-term debt into longer maturities once rates fall
findings.detail: The council is borrowing on short durations (under 5 years) on the bet that long-term rates will fall, at which point it will refinance into longer-dated debt. This strategy exposes the council to refinancing risk if rates remain elevated.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasts are uncertain; if rates do not fall as expected, the council will refinance into more expensive long-term debt, adding to financing pressures already above sustainability thresholds.
findings.figures: Current PWLB rates: 1-year 4.36% (certainty), 5-year 4.76%, 10-year 5.32%, 25-year 5.89%
findings.quote: Officers agree that long term borrowing should be on shorter durations (1-5 years) and then refinance on longer term durations when rates are expected to be lower

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: Cash balances fell to £18.4m from £117m in nine months
findings.detail: While the council explains this as temporary (holiday period, early salary payments), cash balances declined by £98.6m between March and December 2025. Current balances sit 'a little above' the £40m liquidity buffer, leaving limited headroom.
findings.matters: Thin cash reserves relative to £10.5m monthly payroll reduce resilience to timing mismatches or revenue shortfalls; the council is reliant on its liquidity buffer.
findings.figures: Cash 31 March 2025: £117.0m; 31 December 2025: £18.4m; liquidity buffer: £40m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025 the Authority had cash balances of £117.0m, this had reduced to £18.4m by 31 December 2025... Cash levels have increased immediately after the holiday period and currently are a little above the liquidity buffer of £40m

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: HRA financing costs approaching 50% of rental income
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account faces rising debt service costs as a share of rental income, rising from 35.1% to 48.6% by 2028/29. The council notes this creates an 'affordability constraint' on future housing investment.
findings.matters: HRA financial stress limits the council's ability to invest in housing supply and maintenance; HRA debt is secured on housing assets and rents, leaving little room for rent rises without hitting affordability limits for residents.
findings.figures: HRA CFR rising from £430.9m (2024/25) to £729.1m (2028/29); financing cost ratio rising from 35.1% to 48.6% of rental income
findings.quote: With financing costs approaching 50% of rental income, there is an affordability constraint that may limit future investment capacity but is not considered to be unaffordable

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: Total council debt to more than double in four years
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement across all funds (General Fund, regeneration, EFS, HRA and IFRS16 adjustments) is forecast to surge from £716.9m to £1,498.2m. This doubling includes £316m of EFS-related debt.
findings.matters: Rapid debt growth increases refinancing risk, limits future borrowing capacity, and signals structural revenue problems that cannot be solved by capital investment returns alone.

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: General Fund debt is rising rapidly with no offsetting income stream
findings.detail: While regeneration borrowing is offset by rental and other income, service spending borrowing (excluding regeneration) is rising with only modest offset. The Capital Financing Requirement for services grows from £156m to £197m over 4 years, compressed only by Minimum Revenue Provision.
findings.matters: Service borrowing lacks the revenue generation of regeneration schemes; it represents pure cost to the general fund and tax base.
findings.figures: Service spending CFR 2024/25: £156.3m; 2028/29: £197.3m; financing cost ratio 8.2% to 9.2%
findings.quote: Borrowing as a result of service spending over the 4 year period prescribed by the code only increases from £156m in 2024/25 to £197m in 2028/29, less than £10m per year

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: Council Tax being consumed by debt service costs due to government underfunding
findings.detail: As a result of forced EFS borrowing, an increasing share of Council Tax income goes to financing costs rather than services. The ratio rises to 15% by 2028/29, meaning residents' tax bills are funding historical underfunding rather than front-line delivery.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know what portion of a council's tax income is committed to debt service; this trend shows deteriorating headroom for service delivery or further borrowing.
findings.figures: EFS financing costs as % of Council Tax yield: 0.5% (2024/25) rising to 14.0% (2028/29); total GF financing costs rising from 12.1% to 31.3%
findings.quote: Effectively meaning 15% of a residents Council Tax bill is going towards the financing costs due to the Council being underfunded rather than helping support front line services

findings.paper_title: TREASURY MANAGEMENT STRATEGY STATEMENT AND ANNUAL INVESTMENT STRATEGY 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.havering.gov.uk/documents/s82775/TMSS Annual Investment Strategy Audit committe version final 24feb26.pdf
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support borrowing breaches Prudential Code affordability requirements
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that projected borrowing as a result of exceptional financial support does not meet the affordability and sustainability requirements of the CIPFA Prudential Code. The document states this explicitly as a 'full breach' of the code. Unlike the capital programme (which is compliant), the EFS borrowing creates revenue pressures that cannot be absorbed without additional cost-neutral funding.
findings.matters: Prudential Code compliance is a statutory requirement; breach signals structural affordability problems that will constrain future financial flexibility and raise borrowing costs.
findings.figures: EFS borrowing requirement rising from £30m (current) to £346m in 4 years; statutory revenue charge rising from £760k to £28.6m by 2028/29
findings.quote: With no solution to the revenue pressures which is further compounded by the additional financing costs associated with the borrowing for the EFS, unless borrowing specifically for the EFS can be provided with no additional cost to revenue, then the financial situation is simply not affordable nor sustainable. This would be in full breech of the Prudential Code

findings.paper_title: Five Year Capital Programme and Strategy Report 2026/27 - 2030/31
findings.headline: Council adding £5.5m in essential catch-up spending on building safety and condition (asbestos £1.5m, building works £4m).
findings.detail: The new capital projects include £1.5m for corporate estate asbestos removal and £4m for corporate building works, signalling accumulated maintenance backlog. These are described as "essential building safety/condition works" being added to the programme due to "concerns over revenue affordability." This suggests deferred maintenance is now compressing into the capital programme.
findings.matters: Building condition backlogs are typically precursors to larger capital shocks. Essential works being deferred due to affordability concerns indicate the council is managing cash flow tightly.
findings.figures: Asbestos works £1.5m over three years (2026/27-2028/29); building works £4m over two years (2027/28-2028/29)
findings.quote: included within the proposed capital programme is an allocation of £0.6m for parks improvements...Also included within the proposed capital programme are the essential works to the corporate estate buildings (£4m) along with essential Asbestos works (£1.5m)

findings.paper_title: Five Year Capital Programme and Strategy Report 2026/27 - 2030/31
findings.headline: Capital receipts programme is already shortfalling on £30m target by £0.8m, with limited new disposal sites available.
findings.detail: The capital programme assumes £30m in capital receipts (£10m per year for 3 years) to reduce borrowing requirements, but current forecasts show a shortfall of £0.8m. The council has already exhausted most obvious disposals and notes that new sites "becomes more difficult to identify...that do not pose challenges, either technically or in terms of planning." Each £1m shortfall translates to £240k additional annual MTFS pressure.
findings.matters: A structural gap between assumed and achievable capital receipts forces higher borrowing. If targets continue to miss by similar margins, annual revenue pressure accelerates.
findings.figures: £0.8m shortfall on target; £30m three-year receipts target; £240k per annum pressure per £1m shortfall
findings.quote: Current forecasts indicate a shortfall in the capital receipts target of £0.8m although additional sites for disposal are being investigated

findings.paper_title: Five Year Capital Programme and Strategy Report 2026/27 - 2030/31
findings.headline: Capital programme is 65% funded by borrowing (£687m), with council heavily dependent on volatile regeneration income to service debt costs.
findings.detail: Of the £1,050m five-year capital programme, £687m (65%) is funded by prudential borrowing. The council explicitly acknowledges that regeneration income streams are volatile and should not be overrelied upon to balance the budget, yet these projects are essential to offset capital financing costs and generate future revenue returns. Delivery delays or market downturns in regeneration projects would directly impact revenue sustainability.
findings.matters: High leverage combined with reliance on volatile commercial income creates refinancing risk. Any underperformance in regeneration projects (Mercury Land Holdings, Bridge Close, Rainham & Beam Park) directly impacts the council's ability to service debt.
findings.figures: Total borrowing £687.351m over five years; 2026/27 borrowing £121.915m; 2029/30 peaks at £189.051m
findings.quote: income streams can be more volatile than other investments made solely for treasury purposes (details of which are set out in the Treasury Management Strategy Statement (TMSS) elsewhere in the agenda). Members are reminded that over reliance on these income streams should not be made when setting a balanced budget

findings.paper_title: Five Year Capital Programme and Strategy Report 2026/27 - 2030/31
findings.headline: Council has been in Exceptional Financial Support since 2025/26 due to demand pressures and inadequate central government funding.
findings.detail: Havering applied for government support via the Exceptional Financial Support framework in 2025/26 because it could not set a balanced budget otherwise. The council needed £88m EFS support in 2025/26 (with £60m expected to be drawn), and used £30.4m in 2024/25. This creates recurring financing costs of approximately £6m per year over 20 years as the council must borrow to repay the capitalisation direction.
findings.matters: A council needing exceptional government support to balance its budget is a fundamental credit concern. The need to borrow the repayment of EFS creates a structural revenue pressure.
findings.figures: £88m EFS support agreed for 2025/26 (£60m expected to be drawn); £30.4m used in 2024/25; £6m per year additional financing costs for 20 years
findings.quote: the Council has faced rapidly increasing demand pressures in 2025/26 which together with inadequate grant funding from central government has meant that in order to set a balanced budget for 2025/26 (a requirement by statute), the Council has had no choice but to apply for financial support via this framework

editorial.headline: Havering's structural deficit forces £37.7m exceptional support; £240m borrowing conversion ahead
editorial.standfirst: July cabinet papers show Havering's structural deficit requiring exceptional support, as £240m internal borrowing converts to external next year.
editorial.body:
Havering's 2025/26 accounts, presented to July's cabinet, reveal structural revenue collapse. The council's net expenditure reached £242.11m against available funding, "necessitating the use [of] Exceptional Financial Support" of £37.7m. This is not a one-off overspend. The council's own papers describe it as "an underlying budget gap" that already requires further exceptional support budgeted for 2026/27.

The deficit masks systemic failure across core services. Within Living Well, Learning Disabilities overspent by £1.95m despite receiving £4.9m additional growth. The council identifies "complexity pressures" as the culprit—spending on high-cost transition cases and client complexity outpacing new resource. Schools have deteriorated sharply: from a £1.86m surplus at the end of 2024/25 to an overall deficit of £0.72m, with 15 schools now in individual deficit totalling £6.3m.

Capital spending has become the council's chronic drag. Outturn was £135.4m against a £163.7m forecast—a £28.4m shortfall the council attributes to "delayed start on site at four schemes approved to start in 2025/26" across Mercury Land Holdings' housing programme. SEND school expansions were hit by "delays in the procurement process and appointment of contractors." Transport for London schemes went undelivered due to "resourcing constraints," leaving grant funding unclaimed. The council requested £125m carry-forward.

Revenue savings delivery collapsed: £1.2m went unachieved, £2.0m delayed to 2026/27.

The 2026/27 outlook will be defined by debt. The council holds £240m of internal borrowing. Papers note "it is highly likely therefore that further new external borrowing will be needed in 2026/27 both to finance that year's capital programme but also to reduce the level of internal borrowing as those funds are needed for other purposes." This conversion will materially increase debt service costs. The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit stands at £69m; a required £6.9m local contribution hinges on DfE SEND Reform Plan approval.
editorial.pull_quote: increasing levels of client complexity, despite adding in £4.9m of growth
editorial.watch_next: The 2026/27 budget setting will formally confirm the external borrowing requirement and DfE SEND Reform Plan approval status.
